subject: Concordia: tiling strategy, burst handrails and headroom checklist
messages:
From: Jane Roe <jane.roe@concordiasys.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 01 May 2027 09:06:00 -0700
Subject: Concordia capacity request: committed slab sizing for Q3 launch

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the conversation last week — Concordia is moving forward with a committed Dedicated purchase tied to our Q3 rollout and we need a quick sizing and headroom check before procurement. We captured a short token profile (attached) based on our telemetry and a conservative peak we expect during onboarding. Key items: 

- Typical request: 175–250 tokens per API call (most are short prompts + finish).
- Expected steady-state throughput for month 1: 22M tokens/day (~255 tokens/sec avg over 24h).
- Peak bursts during business hours (US): single-region spikes up to ~2,500 tokens/sec sustained for 10–15m; extreme spikes up to ~8,000 tokens/sec for 60–120s during campaigns.
- P95 latency target: 250ms for text-generation (we can tolerate longer tail for background jobs).

We are aiming to sign a 12‑month reserved commitment and would like Redwood's recommendation for: committed slab sizing (GPUs), recommended burst buffer (if any), expected p95 and p99 under the proposed slab, and any graceful-degrade guidance if we hit peaks. Can you also flag the implications for pricing tiers / canary window?

Attachment: concordia_token_profile.csv (CSV)

Would love a short MA P on Mon/Tue to lock the numbers into the contract.

—Jane

Thanks Jane — this is perfect context. Looping in Priyom and Aditya to provide a compact sizing run and tradeoffs. High-level approach we typically use:

1) Map your traffic profile to tokens/sec targets (steady, business-hour peak, extreme microbursts).
2) Choose model variant for serving (we need to confirm what model family you plan to run — open checkpoints vs. Redwood-verified variants change per-GPU throughput).
3) Convert TPS to GPUs using per-GPU token/sec estimates, then apply headroom multiplier + failover reserve.

Quick clarifying Qs so the recommendation matches procurement:
- Which model(s) will you serve in production (name & size)? If multi-model, % split?
- Do you require strict 250ms p95 for all traffic classes or only for interactive calls?
- Any immutability for model pinning (i.e., do you need the exact binary for auditing)?

Proposed next step: Priyom will sketch a 2‑scenario plan (conservative and aggressive) with explicit math and suggested committed slab + burst policy. Aditya will outline pricing/contract implication after we pick the committed GPUs. Can you do a 30m sync Mon at 10am PT?

Cheers,
Kimberly Park
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Concordia capacity request: committed slab sizing for Q3 launch

Hi team — taking Jane's profile and Kim's ask, here are two concrete sizing options with the core math. Assumptions (call these out):
- Model: we assumed a medium-size generator (open checkpoint equivalent to ~12B, running quantized inference on A100-like 80GB fleet). If you choose a smaller 7B-like model, per-GPU throughput will be ~2x–3x higher.
- Measured per-GPU throughput (approx, batch=1 steady):
  • 12B quantized (A100): ~850 tokens/sec per GPU (interactive config)
  • 7B quantized (A100): ~2,200 tokens/sec per GPU
- p95 latency budget target: 250ms; p99 will be higher due to queueing under burst.

Scenario A — Conservative (assume 12B / headroom heavy)
- Target steady TPS: 255 tps (from Jane) -> trivial to serve on 1 GPU but this is steady.
- Business-hour sustained peak: 2,500 tps -> GPUs_needed = ceil(2500 / 850) = 3 GPUs.
- Extreme spike: 8,000 tps for short window -> GPUs_needed_peak = ceil(8000 / 850) = 10 GPUs.
- Apply safety/headroom multiplier: recommended committed slab = 3 * 1.5 = 4.5 -> round up to 5 GPUs committed; recommend burst pool to absorb up to additional 5 GPUs for short spikes (on-demand or reserved burst).
- Expected p95 on committed slab (5 GPUs): with continuous batching + KV cache for repeated prefixes, p95 ~180–260ms for typical requests; p99 ~400–800ms during peaks without burst.

Scenario B — Aggressive (assume 7B / throughput-optimized family)
- Per-GPU = 2,200 tps; sustained peak 2,500 tps -> GPUs_needed = ceil(2500 / 2200) = 2 GPUs.
- Extreme spike 8,000 -> ceil(8000 / 2200) = 4 GPUs.
- Safety factor 1.5 -> committed = 2 * 1.5 = 3 -> round to 3 GPUs; burst buffer = +2 GPUs recommended.
- Expected p95 on committed slab (3 GPUs): p95 ~140–200ms; p99 ~300–500ms at short peaks.

Operational notes / graceful-degrade guidance:
- Prefix/KV caching: enable aggressively for chat threads where users repeat prefixes (reduces token generation by ~20–40% on average).
- Canary routing: route 5–10% of production traffic to a cheaper quantized variant during price-sensitive periods, with automatic fallback to committed slab when quality alerts fire.
- Throttling policy: implement soft throttles for non-interactive jobs (background ingestion) to preserve interactive p95.

Recommendation summary for procurement (first pass):
- If Concordia standardizes on 12B family: commit 5 GPUs, add burst pool of 5 GPUs (monthly reserved + burst on demand).
- If Concordia can adopt 7B equivalent: commit 3 GPUs, burst +2 GPUs.

I can drop these numbers into the redwood-tiling-proposal.xlsx with per-month expected token consumption and price bands for committed vs burst. LMK if you want the raw per-hour cost delta baked into the spreadsheet for the doc.

—Priyom

Subject: Re: Concordia capacity request: committed slab sizing for Q3 launch

Jane / team — thanks Priyom, that breakdown is exactly what procurement needs. A couple of contract/pricing notes:

- Pricing buckets: committed GPUs (monthly reserved) have a per-GPU discount vs on-demand. For the recommended 5 GPU conservative slab we estimate about a 32% unit discount vs burst; for 3 GPUs the discount is ~28% (I'll attach a scenario table).
- Burst wings: recommend a small 12‑month contract that has a committed baseline and a defined burst cushion (e.g., reserve 5 GPUs + rights to burst additional on-demand at pre-agreed rates). That keeps the runway predictable while allowing short-term peaks.
- SLA and credits: if you require p95=250ms for all traffic classes we can bake a stricter SLA but would require higher committed slab or cross-region fallback options.

I've attached the draft SLA runbook and will populate the redwood-tiling-proposal.xlsx with cost bands and month-by-month token burn. If the model family ends up being the 7B-equivalent, the cost delta is meaningful — we should list both options in the contract so Concordia can revise model selection later without a pricing re-negotiation.

Attachments: redwood-tiling-proposal.xlsx (spreadsheet), sla-runbook-v2.pdf (PDF)

If you confirm Monday 10am PT, we'll present the spreadsheet and a quick slide with the final recommendation to lock into procurement.

—Aditya Rao

Kim, Priyom, Aditya — this is great, thank you.

Concordia prefers to standardize on the 12B family for quality reasons but we want the pricing protections for the 7B path in case we need to switch during scaleup. Please proceed with:

- Formal spreadsheet and two-line pricing (12B slab & 7B slab) for procurement by EOD Wed.
- Commit recommendation: we are okay to price-check the conservative plan (commit 5 GPUs + burst 5) if you can provide the per-month cost delta and the SLA credit language.
- I accepted the 10am PT sync — please send calendar invite.

Attachment: none (will use your files)

Best,
Jane
